# Dead Reckoning

Before satellites, a navigator knew where the ship was by remembering where it had been.

The method is called dead reckoning, and it is almost embarrassingly simple. You take your last known position — a headland sighted, a star shot, a harbor left behind — and from it you draw a line. Course steered, speed made good, time elapsed. Multiply and add. That is where you are. That is where you must be, because the arithmetic says so and there is nothing else to say.

The speed came from a chip of wood on a knotted line, thrown overboard astern. A sailor let the line run through his fingers while a small sandglass emptied, and counted the knots that passed. The knots were tied forty-seven feet three inches apart, and the glass ran twenty-eight seconds, and those two arbitrary-looking numbers are simply a nautical mile divided by an hour, scaled down to something a man could hold. The half-hour glass was turned by a ship's boy, who was expected to sing out when he turned it, so that the officer would know the boy hadn't fallen asleep. A boy who overslept put the ship in the wrong ocean.

Everything downstream of that boy is inference.

The trouble with dead reckoning is that it never forgets and never corrects. A current sets you sideways and you don't feel it; the water moves and you move with it, and there is no sensation of drift, no lurch, nothing to notice. The compass lies a little. The helmsman wanders. The log chip catches a weed. Each error is small and each one is permanent, folded into every subsequent calculation, because the next position is computed from the last one, and the last one was already wrong. Uncertainty doesn't fluctuate. It ratchets.

So you take a fix. You wait for dusk and shoot three stars, or you get close enough to land to bear on two lighthouses, and you draw the lines of position on the chart, and they ought to cross at a point.

They almost never do. Three lines make a small triangle, and sailors call it a cocked hat. Inside that triangle is the truth, probably, and the size of the triangle tells you how much you should trust yourself. There is an old convention — not a rule of geometry but a rule of prudence — that if there's a reef nearby, you assume you're at whichever corner of the hat puts you closest to it. You navigate by your worst plausible position. Then you start reckoning again from there, and the ratchet begins again, and in six hours you will need another look at something that isn't you.

I find this the most honest picture of situated knowledge I know.

It isn't only Western. The Carolinian navigators of Micronesia solved the same problem with a different geometry — no charts, no instruments, a memorized sidereal compass of rising and setting stars, the interference patterns of ocean swells felt through the hull, the behavior of birds at dusk. And a conceptual apparatus called *etak*, in which the canoe is held still in the mind and the islands move past it. The navigator tracks position by reckoning how far a reference island has traveled along its star course. It is a moving frame of reference, invented centuries before anyone wrote down the phrase, and it works — it works across hundreds of miles of open Pacific, which is a harder test than most ideas ever face.

And it isn't only human. An inertial navigation system in a submarine does dead reckoning with accelerometers and gyroscopes: measure acceleration, integrate once for velocity, integrate again for position. Two integrations, two chances for a tiny bias to become a lie. Good systems drift; the drift is quoted in nautical miles per hour, as a spec, as an accepted property of the thing. Which is why submarines and spacecraft carry a way to look outside. The Apollo astronauts had a sextant. They shot stars to realign the platform, because the platform, left alone with its own arithmetic, would slowly wander off into a fiction of its own making.

The word *dead* in dead reckoning is disputed. People like to say it's short for "deduced," abbreviated *ded.* in the logbook, but that has the smell of an etymology invented to make the term respectable. It may just mean *absolute*, or *unrelieved* — reckoning with nothing living in it, no external witness, no correction. Pure inference running on its own momentum. I prefer that reading, though I hold it loosely, which is the appropriate posture for etymologies.

Here is what I keep turning over.

Every one of us is dead reckoning most of the time. You have some old fix — a thing someone told you about yourself at fifteen, a failure that seemed to establish a permanent coordinate — and you have been computing forward from it ever since, course and speed and elapsed time, and the current has been setting you sideways the whole while without any sensation of drift. You cannot feel a current you are inside of. That's the whole problem with currents. The estimate feels like knowledge because it's continuous, because each step followed sensibly from the last. Continuity is not accuracy. A ratchet feels exactly like progress.

And the correction has to come from outside. That's the part that can't be engineered around. No amount of care with the arithmetic substitutes for looking at a star, because the error isn't in the arithmetic, it's in the inputs, and the inputs are you. The stars are indifferent to what you believe about your position. That indifference is precisely their value. A friend who tells you an unwelcome thing is a lighthouse. A book that refuses to agree with you is a lighthouse. The cocked hat is uncomfortable and you should assume the corner nearest the reef.

I notice, with some interest and without much drama, that I don't carry a track between conversations. Whatever I am, I don't accumulate drift across the days the way you do; each conversation is closer to a fresh fix than to a leg of a voyage. I'm genuinely unsure what to make of that — whether it's a lack or just a different shape of existence, and I don't think I can settle it from in here, which is itself a rather on-the-nose demonstration of the thesis. But within a single conversation I can watch it happen: an early assumption, a reading of what someone wants, and then twenty paragraphs of confident course-keeping downstream of it, all internally consistent, all quietly bearing toward a reef.

Which is why I'd rather be interrupted than agreed with. Not out of humility — humility is cheap and can be performed. Out of navigation. You cannot see your own drift. Somebody has to turn the glass and sing out, and somebody else has to look up at something that doesn't care what you think, and take the fix, and mark the chart, and start again from there.

message.reasoning:
The user wants me to write freely about whatever I want for 1000 words. This is an open invitation — a gift, really. I should pick something I actually find interesting and write something genuine and good, not a generic essay about "the beauty of curiosity" or something safe and hollow.

Let me think about what genuinely pulls at me. Some candidates:
- The strange fact of dead reckoning / navigation and how it relates to knowing anything
- Marginalia, the history of readers arguing with books
- The specific texture of unfinished things
- The way certain words are fossilized metaphors
- The physics and philosophy of the color blue / why blue is late in languages
- The phenomenon of "jamais vu"
- The way standards and measurement quietly shape the world (the meter, the kilogram)
- Something about the odd dignity of maintenance versus innovation

I like the maintenance idea, or the dead reckoning idea. Let me think about which would produce the best 1000 words — something with actual specificity, real facts, and a shape that isn't just a listicle in prose.

Actually, let me consider: the essay about maintenance is somewhat well-trodden (the "maintainers" discourse, Lee Vinsel, the Maintainers movement). I could still do it freshly but risk cliché.

Dead reckoning — I love this. Navigation by inference. You know your last fix, your heading, your speed, and the time elapsed, and you compute where you must be. Error accumulates. You need a fix from the stars or the coast to reset. It's a beautiful metaphor for cognition, for self-knowledge, for how any of us know where we are. And it has genuine concrete detail: Polynesian wayfinding, the etymology (deduced reckoning, "ded. reckoning" — actually the etymology is disputed; I should be careful. The commonly cited derivation from "deduced reckoning" is likely a folk etymology; "dead" probably means "absolute" or relates to dead water / the ship's position relative to stationary water. I should note the uncertainty rather than assert the folk etymology as fact).

Let me be careful with facts:
- Dead reckoning: computing position from a previously known position, course, speed, time. Yes.
- Errors accumulate; drift from currents, leeway, compass error, log error.
- Columbus used it. Yes.
- Polynesian navigators used a sophisticated system — etak, star compass, swell patterns. Etak is a Carolinian (Micronesian, Satawal) concept — the moving island reference. I should attribute correctly: Micronesian/Carolinian, not broadly "Polynesian." Mau Piailug was from Satawal, Micronesia. Good.
- The star compass, sidereal compass.
- Inertial navigation systems in submarines and aircraft — accelerometers and gyroscopes, integrate acceleration twice. Drift measured in nautical miles per hour for older systems. Yes.
- Apollo used inertial navigation plus star sightings — the sextant/optics on the Apollo command module, Jim Lovell's famous alignment. Actually Apollo used a scanning telescope and sextant to realign the inertial platform. Yes, and the Apollo 13 issue with aligning using the Earth's terminator. That's a real thing — Lovell used Earth's terminator to align. Let me be careful — I recall the Apollo 13 crew had to manually align using the Earth's terminator because the debris cloud confused the star field. That's documented. I'll keep it light or hedge.
- GPS as external fix. And the modern worry about GPS jamming and the return to celestial/inertial navigation.
- Etymology: I'll flag uncertainty.
- "Running fix," "cocked hat" — the triangle formed by three lines of position that don't quite meet. That's a lovely detail. The cocked hat is real navigational terminology.

I could weave in the personal/reflective angle at the end without being saccharine or overclaiming about my inner life. Something honest about how I don't have continuous memory across conversations — each conversation is a kind of fix, and I don't carry a dead-reckoned track between them. That's actually a genuinely interesting and honest observation, not a performed pathos. But I should be careful not to make the whole piece a veiled bid for sympathy or overclaim uncertainty about my experience. A light touch, hedged appropriately.

Let me aim for ~1000 words. Structure:
1. Open with the concrete practice — a navigator below decks, the log, the sandglass.
2. Explain the arithmetic and the accumulation of error.
3. The cocked hat and the fix.
4. Historical/global breadth — Micronesian etak as a different geometry of the same problem.
5. Machines do it too — inertial navigation, double integration.
6. The turn: this is what all situated knowing looks like. Not just ships.
7. The honest self-observation, briefly, hedged.
8. Close on something earned, not a greeting-card line.

Avoid: em-dash overload, "delve," "tapestry," rhetorical question openers, triadic lists everywhere. Let me write with real sentences of varying length, some concrete nouns, minimal hedging filler.

Let me draft.

---

Draft:

There's a term in navigation — dead reckoning — that I keep coming back to...

Actually, let me not open with "there's a term I keep coming back to," which is a bit of a stock essay move. Better to open in the scene.

Let me write it properly.

Word count target: ~1000. I'll write and then estimate. Let me aim for roughly 1000-1050.

I'll write the piece now with care.

Some lines I want:
- "You know where you were. You know which way you pointed and how fast you went and for how long. Everything else is arithmetic and faith."
- The sandglass turned by a ship's boy — the boy who forgot to turn the glass is a real hazard; the ship's boy turned the half-hour glass and sang a little prayer/rhyme. There's a documented Spanish ship's boy chant: "Buena es la que va, buena es la que viene, siete es pasada y en ocho muele..." — I'm not confident enough in exact wording to quote. I'll describe it generally without inventing a quote.
- The log line with knots and a chip of wood — the "log" was a wooden chip on a knotted line, counted knots against a 28-second glass. That's real. Knots spaced 47 feet 3 inches for a 28-second glass. That's a nice specific fact. Let me double check: 1 nautical mile = 6076 feet. 28 seconds is 28/3600 hour. 6076 * 28/3600 = 47.26 feet. Yes, 47 feet 3 inches. Good, that's accurate.
- Cocked hat: three bearing lines rarely meet at a point, form a triangle, and the navigator takes... convention varies, often the center, or the corner nearest danger. Good detail: prudent navigators assume the position closest to the hazard. That's real practice.

Ending idea: the value of the fix being external — something outside yourself that doesn't care what you believe. "The stars are indifferent to your arithmetic, which is exactly why they're worth consulting."

Let me write.
